newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Tokyo stocks erode, HK hit by rate fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tokyo stocks erode, HK hit by rate fears.

text.p: Tokyo stocks shed more than three percent on Thursday to close at the lowest level in over a year after a key business leader warned of "grave problems" if the market continues to fall.
Hong Kong stocks also slumped amid concern over rising U.S. interest rates and fears the government could impose measures to curb growing property speculation, which hurt property shares.
Tokyo's key 225-share Nikkei average fell 606.51 points, or 3.25 percent, to 18,073.87. Dealers said the fall brought it one step closer to the next psychological support level of 18,000.
Bank shares in Tokyo in particular were under pressure on Thursday, which pulled other sectors down.

A senior official at Japan's Ministry of Finance told Reuters the country's economy is not in as bad a state as the stock market thinks. However, Jiji news agency quoted the chairman of the Japan Chamber of Commerce as saying Japan will face "grave problems" before Japanese banks close their books for the fiscal year if stocks continue to fall.
The comment prompted the sharp drop, which extended the Nikkei's earlier loss of more than 500 points.
Brokers have been concerned that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will do little to help an already nascent economic recovery while implementing needed structural reforms.
The drop in stock prices, which trim unrealized profits on bank's stock holdings, has added to investors concerns over local banks, which bear the the burden of massive problem loans.
Hong Kong stocks in part took their cue from a jittery U.S. government bond market, where the key 30-year bond fell 21/32 to 95-20/32, pushing the yield up to 6.84 percent on Wednesday.
The rise in rates reflected concern about upcoming U.S. economic data, such as the producer price and jobs data due Thursday and Friday, respectively.
Hong Kong stocks extended their heavy losses in Thursday afternoon trade, with the Hang Seng index tumbling more than 300 points within minutes of reopening after the midsession break.
By 0710 GMT the index had clawed back some ground but was still down 287.90 points at 13167.03.
In Taiwan, shares ended slightly lower after a firmer opening as trading turned volatile due to the launch of offshore Taiwan stock futures in Singapore and Chicago.
The index was off 8.67 points, or 0.12 percent, at 7,010.76.
Brokers said the impact of the futures moves abroad was weaker than expected, probably because Taiwan regulators still forbid local investors to trade the foreign contracs.
"Our hypersensitive local investors should get used to them pretty soon. In the long run, all price movements should return to fundamentals," said Jardine Fleming fund manager George Hou.
The March contract of the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) Taiwan index ended at 307.3 against its opening 299.7 after hitting a high of 311.0. Only 500 lots changed hangds.
Elsewhere in Asia, Thai stocks were higher amid hopes that planned government spending cuts would boost the troubled economy. The SET index was up 10.09 points, or 1.21 percent, at 842.02.

Despite growing labour unrest Korean stocks jumped 2.97 percent, propelled by a rise in bank stocks and a growing sentiment the market may have reached bottom. The composite index closed at a provisional 639.87, or 18.46 points higher.
Stocks have been hard hit by massive strikes throughout the country.
In Singapore, stocks gained 3.17 points, or 0.14 percent, to 2,246.43, while Malaysian stocks were off 4.87 points, or 0.39 percent, at 1,234.67.
Indonesian shares lost 4.65 points, or 0.70 percent, to 657.56 and Philippine stocks were up 16.37 points, or 0.51 percent, at 3,223.36.
Australian stocks were up 8.2 points, or 0.34 percent at 2,423.2, while New Zealand shares gained 3.05 points, or 0.13 percent, to 2,402.36.
